activities.anchor: the Irish potato famine is the classic case
activities.caption: pair each level of biodiversity with what it counts
activities.name: bdcLevelsMatch

config.prompt: Three levels plus two measures — pair each term with its meaning:

pairs.right: variation within a species — the raw material for adaptation
how evenly individuals are spread among the species
the variety of habitats and their processes

config.why: The levels erode together: lose habitat and you lose species; lose species and surviving populations shrink and inbreed. A genetically uniform crop meeting a disease it cannot evade is the classic failure case.

activities.caption: rebuild the rainforest's vertical stack, top down
activities.name: bdcCanopyOrder

config.prompt: A tropical rainforest stacks life vertically — put the layers in order, highest first:
items: Emergent crowns breaking through the top
Canopy — the continuous main ceiling of leaves
Floor — thin litter over paradoxically poor soil
config.why: Each layer adds niches, which is why the stacking multiplies species. And the fertility lives in the biomass, not the ground: clear-cut and the nutrient capital leaves with the timber and the first rains.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the extinction arithmetic
activities.name: bdcExtinctSpot

config.prompt: This summary of the extinction arithmetic contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The background rate, read from the fossil record, runs at roughly 0.1–1 extinctions per million species per year.
Mammals today are disappearing at least tens of times that background rate.
A tenfold gain in area roughly doubles the species count.
So shrinking a forest to 10% of its area leaves about 10% of its species standing.
Many species already doomed by past clearing have not yet vanished — the extinction debt.
config.correction: With the species–area exponent near 0.25, 10% of the area retains 0.1^0.25 ≈ 56% of species — and eventually loses roughly half.
config.why: The loss follows a power law, not a straight ratio: that gap between 10% and 56% is exactly why the word 'eventually' carries the argument.

activities.anchor: the hotspots strategy is conservation triage by arithmetic
activities.caption: true or false — the drivers and the map
activities.name: bdcDriverJudge

statements.s: A species found in the Tropical Andes and nowhere else on Earth is endemic there.
statements.why: Endemic means found nowhere else — which is why hotspot hectares carry outsized stakes.

statements.s: The five drivers act independently: halving one leaves the other four untouched.
statements.why: They compound — a fragmented, warming, over-harvested population loses the genetic diversity that might have let it adapt.

statements.s: Rats and cats arriving on islands are a historic cause of island extinctions.
statements.why: Invasive species rank as the second-greatest historic cause of island extinctions.

statements.s: The hotspots strategy spreads scarce conservation money evenly across all regions.
statements.why: It is triage by arithmetic: most endemic species in the smallest areas get targeted first.

activities.anchor: every halving of habitat has a predictable species price
activities.caption: which curve prices the habitat cut?
activities.name: bdcAreaTrace

config.prompt: A forest island is cut to a fraction x of its area. Which curve tracks the fraction of species remaining when the island exponent z ≈ 0.25?
config.why: S ∝ A^0.25: cut to 10% and 0.1^0.25 ≈ 0.56 of species remain — about half — while the 1:1 rule would have predicted a ruinous 10%.

activities.anchor: Bleached reefs can recover in weeks if the heat passes
activities.caption: the reef manager's heatwave — trace your choices
activities.name: bdcReefBranch

config.root: You manage a marine protected area. The forecast says a marine heatwave is bearing down on your reef.

start.text: The heatwave hits: the corals expel their algae and turn white, alive but starving. Your move?

choices.label: Cut local stress now — protect herbivorous fish, halt nutrient runoff
choices.feedback: Buys recovery time: grazers keep algae off the skeleton while the partnership re-forms.

choices.label: Declare the reef dead and move the budget elsewhere
choices.feedback: A breakdown is not a burial — white coral is starving, not gone.

choices.label: Hold local funds and wait for global emissions policy to arrive
choices.feedback: Warming sets the ceiling — but nothing is left to save if the reef is fished bare meanwhile.

local.text: If the heat passes, colour can return within weeks. But the real enemy is frequency: consecutive heat years kill — which is why you watch bleaching frequency, not any single event.

dead.text: The 2016 event bleached about half the Great Barrier Reef's corals, and many recovered. Reefs are built by animals in partnership with algae — and the partnership can resume.

global.text: Reefs carry every driver at once — warming, acidification, runoff, overfished grazers. Local action cannot lower the ceiling, but it decides whether anything survives beneath it.

config.why: The local interventions that work buy time without solving the warming that sets the ceiling — reef conservation is the field's hardest systems problem.

activities.caption: two parks, one budget — drag between the models
activities.name: bdcFenceCompare

config.prompt: Who guards the park? Drag the divider:

before.label: fortress park
before.text: Fences first, people excluded. Strictly fenced 'fortress' parks repeatedly underperform — because poaching is an economics problem, and fences do not change economics.

after.label: community-led landscape
after.text: Local communities hold rights and earn from wildlife — tourism, hunting quotas, forest products. Enforcement with local buy-in is the strongest predictor of a protected area's success.

config.why: Governance matters as much as gazetting: aligning local incentives with enforcement is what makes boundaries hold.

activities.anchor: the California condor fell to 27 in 1987
activities.caption: call the recovery — from 27 birds
activities.name: bdcCondorEstimate

config.prompt: The California condor fell to 27 birds in 1987, every one taken into captivity. Roughly how many fly free again today?
config.why: Over 500 — species-level rescue has a perfect and a dramatic record when habitat and threats are handled alongside the captive programme.
config.context: The Mauritius kestrel made the same climb: four known individuals in 1974, hundreds now.
